transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Jared Collins (Meridian - Head of Data Platform), Maya Ruiz (Meridian - Security Architect), Tom Bennett (Meridian - Cloud Ops)

Summary: Short scoping call to nail down private networking approach and POC success criteria for Meridian Health's LLM inference workloads. Focus on avoiding PHI egress, region restrictions, and measurable benchmark targets.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Alex, AE on the account; with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. Quick check, is this still a good time?
[00:08] Jared (Meridian): Yep all good, Jared here. Thanks Alex. We'll let Maya and Tom chime in on security and networking later.
[00:15] Priya (Redwood): Hi all, yep, my role here is to map out the benchmark and the network options. We're expecting this call to be mostly scoping: success criteria, network topology, and timeline.
[00:26] Maya (Meridian): Great, quick context: Meridian runs patient-facing apps with PHI. Any POC must ensure no PHI leaves our VPC or leaves the region. We have strong egress controls and need KMS integration.
[00:40] Tom (Meridian): Also want clarity on whether we need NAT gateways for egress and any implications for cost — egress charges are a thing for us.
[00:50] Alex: Totally understood. From Redwood's side, we support Private deployments and private networking via VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink — both are viable; there are tradeoffs which we'll walk through.
[01:05] Priya: Quick high level: VPC peering is simple routes between VPCs, low latency, but you need to manage route tables, and transitive peering doesn't work. PrivateLink creates an interface endpoint in your VPC to our service, which is more controlled and often preferred by security teams because it avoids route-table changes.
[01:25] Jared: Okay — for us, security prefers PrivateLink, but we've seen teams go with peering for high-throughput because PrivateLink has ENI limits and costs.
[01:36] Priya: Right — PrivateLink does attach ENIs in subnets and scales, but there's a per-GB and per-hour cost. For the POC we can estimate both. We should get your expected throughput to size it.
[01:52] Maya: Throughput — target is about 2 million tokens/day initially, with peaks up to 200 requests per second for short bursts. Latency SLO: p95 under 200ms is our goal for snappy UX.
[02:07] Priya: Great detail. For benchmarking we'll model sequence lengths — what are average and max token lengths?
[02:14] Jared: Average is around 150 tokens, max 1,200 for some clinical summaries. But most production calls are sub-300.
[02:22] Priya: Good to know — that affects KV cache footprint and memory. For a private deployment we'll likely recommend a quantized model variant for cost; for latency-sensitive flows we might use a slightly larger instance class.
[02:35] Tom: Can you explain KV cache — is that something that stays in memory on the Redwood nodes or in our VPC?
[02:43] Priya: KV cache is per-inference instance memory to accelerate autoregressive sampling; it lives on the serving nodes. In Private deployments the nodes run in your VPC (or in a customer-dedicated VPC), so the cache doesn't leave your network — but the control plane still coordinates model versions unless you opt for an air-gapped control plane.
[03:02] Maya: Air-gapped might be necessary for some PHI flows. We need to check legal — but initial POC can be with a private control plane, assuming logs and telemetry do not contain PHI.
[03:14] Alex: We'll document what telemetry is sent by default. We also support field-level filtering and log redaction for POCs.
[03:21] Jared: Back to networking: we need region constraints — primary region will be us-east-1. We might want eu-west-1 for DR, but data residency in EU only applies to a narrower subset.
[03:33] Priya: For DR, we can provision a second deployment in eu-west-1; we can also do a control-plane-in-us with data-plane-only in eu if that's required. We'll clarify options in the follow-up doc.
[03:45] Maya: Important: no egress to internet from the inference nodes. All model downloads and any external calls need to be inside our VPC or via approved endpoints.
[03:56] Priya: Understood. For model artifacts, Redwood can seed models into a private S3 bucket in your account or we can pull, but in that case you'd want to ensure the pull is from within your VPC. We can also support pre-baked AMIs or container images to avoid external pulls.
[04:14] Tom: If we do VPC peering, do we still need NAT Gateway for third-party telemetry? We're trying to avoid NAT costs.
[04:23] Alex: You won't need NAT for the Redwood service traffic if peering or PrivateLink is set up. NAT comes in if nodes need to access external services on the internet. For POC we can route model artifact staging through a secured S3 endpoint (VPC endpoint) so NAT not required.
[04:38] Jared: Benchmark behavior — how do you run it? We want realistic load: concurrent streams, varied sequence lengths, and cold/warm KV cache differences.
[04:49] Priya: Our standard benchmark plan for POC: 1) Warmup phase with synthetic traffic to populate KV cache; 2) Steady-state run at target concurrency for 30–60 minutes; 3) Burst tests for short windows to emulate traffic spikes; 4) End-to-end latency and tokencost metrics captured at p50/p95/p99. We'll provide a script you can run from your VPC or we can run it from Redwood nodes connecting via the PrivateLink/peering endpoint — recommended is running from your VPC to avoid cross-network variability.
[05:18] Maya: If you run from Redwood's side we need to be confident traffic never traverses public internet.
[05:24] Priya: Correct, we will test over the private endpoint. For the POC we'll provide a benchmark harness that you can execute in your environment.
[05:31] Tom: On the model side, are you serving open models or do you host our proprietary fine-tuned model? We will be testing with some proprietary vectors and might require model encryption at rest.
[05:41] Priya: We can serve both. For proprietary models, we can host in your account or in a customer-controlled S3 bucket and run inference in your VPC, and we support KMS customer-managed keys for encryption at rest.
[05:53] Maya: KMS integration is must-have. Also audit logs retention — we need logs retained for 12 months and editable retention windows.
[06:03] Alex: We can support audit log forwarding to your SIEM via VPC endpoints; retention windows can be configured. We'll include specifics in the security questionnaire.
[06:12] Jared: Let's capture POC success criteria now so everyone aligns: 1) No PHI egress outside allowed regions; 2) p95 latency <200ms for standard flows; 3) sustain 2M tokens/day with 200 rps bursts; 4) KMS-managed encryption at rest; 5) ability to run benchmark inside our VPC. Anything to add?
[06:31] Maya: Add that audit logs must be forwardable and that PrivateLink is preferred unless peering needed for throughput.
[06:38] Tom: Also include a cost target — we don't need exact numbers but an order of magnitude for per-token cost vs hosted. Let's mark that as a secondary success criterion.
[06:47] Alex: Good list. We'll put those into the SOW and POC plan.
[06:52] Priya: On timeline: typical POC for private networking is 4–6 weeks: week 1 network setup (peering/PrivateLink + endpoints + IAM), week 2 model staging and small validation, weeks 3–4 benchmark runs and tuning, week 5 deliverables and wrap. If you need faster we can compress but we'd need dedicated support.
[07:12] Jared: 4 weeks sounds acceptable. Budget approval is in progress; timeline likely aligns.
[07:18] Maya: A couple of nitty-gritty networking questions: route table propagation and whether we need to touch on cross-account role setup.
[07:26] Priya: For peering, you update route tables to point to the peer. For PrivateLink, we create an NLB on our side and you create interface endpoints in your subnets — then security groups control access. For cross-account, we'll need a role or acceptance flow; we'll include step-by-step in the network checklist.
[07:44] Tom: Regarding ENI limits for PrivateLink, do you have recommendations for subnet sizing?
[07:50] Priya: Yes — we'll recommend at least two subnets with enough ENI capacity for the expected concurrency. We'll provide a worksheet where you put expected rps and sequence lengths and it outputs recommended instance count and subnet sizing.
[08:03] Jared: On data residency, if we have to keep EU data in eu-west-1, how does the control plane work?
[08:11] Alex: We have two modes — control plane in Redwood's cloud with a private data plane in your region, or an optional Private control plane hosted in your account for stricter requirements. For the POC we can do the hybrid: control plane in us-east but all inference and logs in eu-west for the EU subset. We'll document the tradeoffs.
[08:31] Maya: For compliance we'll want proof that logs don't cross borders for EU records — is filtering available per-tenant or per-route?
[08:39] Priya: We support per-route tenancy and log partitioning. We'll need to see how you tag EU traffic but yes, partitioning is possible.
[08:48] Tom: Any special firewall or proxy rules? We run a corporate proxy for outbound traffic.
[08:54] Priya: If you use an outbound proxy, nodes will need to be able to reach the PrivateLink endpoint or peer subnet; proxy configuration is needed only for internet-bound traffic. For S3 endpoints and internal services, no proxy required.
[09:07] Jared: Let's talk benchmarks specifics: Priya, can you lay out the inputs you need to size and the outputs you provide?
[09:12] Priya: Inputs: average & max seq length, tokens/day, p95 latency target, concurrency/burst profile, model family and quantization preference, regional placement. Outputs: recommended instance types, cluster size for steady-state and burst capacity, expected p95/p99 from prior runs, token cost estimate, and a runbook for running the harness. We'll also provide raw logs and dashboards from the run.
[09:33] Maya: For the runbook, we'd like to see exact curl/sdk commands so we can run it inside our CI or from a bastion.
[09:40] Priya: We'll include curl examples and a small python harness. We also have a k6-based workload generator if you want to reproduce at scale.
[09:47] Tom: On isolation — in Dedicated mode do we get dedicated GPU pools? Is that required for our workload?
[09:53] Alex: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and higher throughput guarantees; Private deployments can be dedicated or shared depending on your commit. For the POC we typically run on a small dedicated slice to emulate production.
[10:06] Jared: Pricing — we'll need a ballpark for PrivateLink + dedicated capacity.
[10:11] Alex: We'll provide a pricing guide in the follow-up SOW; for the POC we can provide trial credits or a short-term commit to de-risk.
[10:19] Maya: One more security question: can you support customer-managed keys (CMKs) in our account for model artifacts and logs?
[10:26] Priya: Yes, we support CMKs. We'll capture the exact IAM trust policy required.
[10:31] Tom: For the POC, we need a simple checklist: CIDR ranges, subnets, security groups, IAM role, S3 bucket for model artifacts, and expected test client IPs.
[10:42] Alex: We'll send that checklist and a network diagram template.
[10:46] Jared: Ok sounds good.
[10:48] Priya: Quick note on monitoring — Redwood Console gives per-route latency and token cost breakdown; for Private deployments we can forward metrics to your CloudWatch or Prometheus via private endpoints.
[11:01] Maya: We'll prefer CloudWatch and our SIEM.
[11:04] Priya: Noted.
[11:06] Alex: Anything else on the technical side?
[11:09] Jared: Might be useful to run a short smoke test within a day or two to validate connectivity before the full benchmark.
[11:15] Alex: Agreed — propose a connectivity smoke test within 48 hours after you share CIDRs. That will validate endpoints, routing, and IAM.
[11:23] Tom: We'll share CIDRs and contact for network team by tomorrow EOD.
[11:28] Maya: Security team will review the SOW and questionnaire; expect comments in 3 business days.
[11:34] Alex: Great. Let's outline explicit POC success criteria and timeline now to close the meeting.
[11:40] Priya: Recap success criteria: 1) No PHI egress outside allowed regions; 2) p95 latency <200ms for standard flows (150 tokens); 3) sustain 2M tokens/day with 200 rps bursts; 4) CMK encryption at rest; 5) Audit logs forwarded and retained 12 months.
[11:58] Jared: Approved. Add secondary: cost estimate within acceptance threshold.
[12:03] Alex: Timeline: Week 0 (this week) - share CIDR & security doc; Week 1 - network setup & smoke test; Week 2 - model staging & small validation; Weeks 3-4 - benchmark runs and tuning; Week 5 - deliverables and decision.
[12:21] Maya: That works.
[12:23] Alex: Okay next steps (we'll email these): send VPC diagram + PrivateLink guide (Alex), benchmark plan (Priya), Meridian provides CIDR + network contact (Tom), security input (Maya).
[12:34] Jared: Thanks everyone.
[12:36] Priya: Thanks — we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark run.
[12:41] Maya: Bye.
[12:43] Tom: Bye.

Action items (as discussed):
- Alex to send VPC peering and PrivateLink diagrams + network checklist
- Priya to deliver benchmark harness and sizing worksheet
- Tom to share CIDR blocks and network contact
- Maya to share security requirements and KMS details

End of transcript.
